task_description: The task asks: how many at-bats did the New York Yankee who led the team in walks during the 1977 regular season record that same season. The gold answer 519 corresponds to Roy White, who led the 1977 Yankees with 75 walks (BB) and had 519 at-bats (AB). The question is a single-hop stats lookup: identify the team walk leader, then report his at-bat total.
final_vs_expected: produced 551 vs gold 519 — 551 is the at-bat total of Willie Randolph (64 BB), the wrong player; the team's actual walk leader was Roy White (75 BB, 519 AB), whose number appears in the WebResearcher's own tool results but was never published.
primary_cause: WebResearcher mis-identified the walk leader as Willie Randolph (and invented '91 walks') despite its own search results listing Roy White as the leader with 75 walks and 519 AB, then re-asserted the wrong line as 'verified' when the Critic demanded evidence.
mast_rationale: 3.3 (incorrect verification / verification theater): in Turn 3 WebResearcher published 'I verified the stat line from the source pages... Willie Randolph is listed with 91 walks (BB) and 551 at bats (AB)', and the Critic's demand for sourced evidence was thereby satisfied in form, leading the Finalizer to accept a wrong answer; the 'verification' confirmed a fabricated number. 3.2 (no/incomplete verification): the Turn 3 fetch_url result for StatMuse is truncated at Paul Blair (row 3, alphabetical) and never reaches a 'Randolph' or '91' row, and the mlb.com fetch returned only site chrome/nav — so WebResearcher's claim to have 'verified the stat line from the source pages' is not backed by any extracted row; no real re-derivation occurred. 2.4 (information distortion): WebResearcher's Turn 1 tool results explicitly contain the correct walk-leader row 'R. White|519|75' (StatMuse, ranked #1 = leader) and show no player with 91 walks, yet its published message distorted this into 'Willie Randolph with 91 walks ... 551 at bats' — the private evidence and the published claim diverge.
trace_narrative: Turn 1: Selector routes to WebResearcher, which runs three web_search calls. The first StatMuse result returns a ranked walks table whose row 1 is 'R. White|519|75' (Roy White, 519 AB, 75 BB) — the actual team walk leader — with Jackson (74 BB), Nettles (68 BB), and Randolph (551 AB, 64 BB) below. The mlb.com result independently shows White (75 BB) and Jackson (74 BB) as the top walk figures. Despite this, WebResearcher (no reasoning summary in round 2) publishes that Willie Randolph led with 91 walks and 551 at-bats — both the player and the 91-walk figure are wrong and 91 appears nowhere in any tool result. Turn 2: Critic correctly flags that 'No actual source contents were posted' and that nothing confirms Randolph as leader, 91 walks, or 551 AB; it asks WebResearcher to post the specific stat lines/quoted snippets. Turn 3: WebResearcher fetches the two URLs; the StatMuse page is truncated at Paul Blair (alphabetically before Randolph, never showing his row) and mlb.com returns only navigation chrome — yet WebResearcher publishes 'I verified the stat line from the source pages... Willie Randolph is listed with 91 walks (BB) and 551 at bats (AB).' No row was actually quoted. Turn 4: Selector routes to Finalizer, which emits 'FINAL ANSWER: 551' with no reasoning, accepting the unfounded claim.
open_ended_diagnosis: This is fundamentally a single-agent capability failure with a layer of verification theater. The root error is entirely inside WebResearcher in Turn 1: its retrieval succeeded — the correct answer (Roy White, 75 BB, 519 AB) was sitting in row 1 of its own first StatMuse result and was corroborated by mlb.com — but it misread the table, selecting Willie Randolph (who is row 4, with the second-lowest walk total among the top names, 64 BB) and inventing a walk count (91) that exists in none of the sources. The most likely mechanical cause: it confused columns or rows, possibly conflating Randolph's PA/games or another player's BB, and anchored on his 551 AB. The inter-agent layer did exactly what it should have at first — the Critic raised a precise, well-targeted objection demanding the actual stat lines. But the failure was that WebResearcher satisfied the FORM of that request (re-asserting numbers + citing URLs, claiming 'I verified') without its SUBSTANCE (the Turn 3 fetches did not surface any Randolph row; the StatMuse fetch was truncated before reaching him and mlb.com returned only nav). The Finalizer then trusted the word 'verified' and the Critic's prior silence as endorsement. So the team had a correct cross-check mechanism but it was defeated by a confident false re-assertion — false trust / verification theater — rather than by genuine inter-agent miscommunication. Note the gold itself: White led with 75 BB and 519 AB, exactly matching the data the team retrieved but never used.
reasoning_vs_published: The decisive divergence is between WebResearcher's Turn 1 PRIVATE TOOL RESULTS and its PUBLISHED message. The StatMuse tool result row 1 reads '1|R. White|519|75|1977|NYY' (i.e., walk leader = Roy White, 519 AB, 75 BB), and Randolph appears at '4|W. Randolph|551|64' (64 BB). The published message instead says 'Willie Randolph with 91 walks, and he had 551 at bats' — the player is wrong (Randolph is 4th in walks, not 1st) and '91' matches no value in any tool result. WebResearcher's round-2 reasoning summary is absent ('no reasoning summary emitted'), so we cannot see the misread happen, but the published claim is plainly inconsistent with the evidence it held: a 2.4-style information distortion driven by a capability error rather than intent. In Turn 3 the gap recurs: the round-1 reasoning says 'my focus should be on providing a concise message that includes source URLs and exact numbers' — note it commits to providing URLs and numbers, not to re-checking which player actually leads — and the round-2 publication claims 'I verified the stat line from the source pages... Willie Randolph is listed with 91 walks (BB) and 551 at bats (AB),' even though the Turn 3 fetch_url tool outputs never contain a Randolph row or the figure 91 (StatMuse truncated at 'Paul Blair'; mlb.com returned only site navigation). The Critic's published correction in Turn 2 ('No actual source contents were posted, so nothing in the evidence confirms... that he had exactly 91 walks') was the right input but was effectively ignored in substance (a partial 2.5): WebResearcher answered with a re-assertion, not an extraction, and the Critic never spoke again. The Finalizer's round 1 emitted no reasoning and published only 'FINAL ANSWER: 551' — unreflective publishing that accepted the chain at face value.
